name: Proverbs
v: The loner chases his own cravings; he picks a fight with every sound principle.
Fools take no joy in understanding — only in broadcasting their opinions.
Where wickedness walks in, contempt follows; with disgrace comes shame trailing behind.
The words of a person are deep waters — but wisdom's source is a rushing stream.
Tilting the scales for the guilty, crushing the innocent in court — both are crimes against justice.
A fool's lips drag him into conflict; his mouth is asking for a beating.
A fool's mouth is his ruin; his lips are a trap that snaps shut on his own soul.
Gossip slides down like a delicacy — straight to the gut, where it lodges forever.
Slack on the job? You're a cousin to the saboteur.
The name of the Lord is a fortified tower — the righteous sprint inside and stand untouchable.
The rich man's wealth is his stronghold — at least, that's the wall he imagines around himself.
Before the crash comes the swollen heart; before the honor comes the bowed head.
Answer before you listen, and you've already made a fool of yourself.
A strong spirit can carry a sick body — but a crushed spirit, who can lift that?
The discerning mind hunts for knowledge; wise ears are always reaching for more.
A gift opens doors — even the doors of the powerful.
The first to speak sounds right — until the cross-examination begins.
When two parties deadlock, casting lots breaks the stalemate, even between the strong.
A brother you've wronged is harder to win than a walled city; their resistance bars the gate.
What comes out of your mouth fills your belly; you eat the harvest of your words.
Life and death sit on the tongue — those who love it will swallow what it serves.
Find a wife and you've found something good — favor pouring down from the Lord.
The poor man begs; the rich man barks back.
Some companions will tear you apart — but a true friend sticks closer than blood.

com.d:
# Proverbs 18: The Power of Our Words and Wisdom

This chapter reveals how profoundly our words shape our lives and relationships, and how the pursuit of wisdom determines whether we live in blessing or self-inflicted harm.

The opening verses establish a sobering truth: "A fool's lips bring him strife, and his mouth invites a beating" (v. 6). Words carry real consequences. We've all experienced how careless speech creates distance, wounds, and conflict—sometimes requiring years to repair. Yet just verses later comes the counterpoint: "The words of the wise bring healing" (v. 4). This isn't poetic exaggeration; words truly do possess creative and destructive power. When we speak with thoughtfulness, kindness, and truth, we build trust and restore broken places. When we speak rashly from pride or anger, we dismantle what took years to construct.

What makes this chapter so practical is how it diagnoses the root problem. A fool doesn't merely speak poorly; he's someone "who delights in airing his own opinions" (v. 15). There's the trap—an unwillingness to listen. Wisdom, by contrast, begins with listening. Verse 13 warns that "a man who answers before listening—that is his folly and shame." The humble person asks questions, seeks counsel, and weighs their words before speaking. They understand that their perspective is incomplete and that listening to others—especially those wiser or different from themselves—is an investment in growth.

The chapter also reminds us that our reputations precede us. "A good name is more desirable than great riches; to be esteemed is better than silver or gold" (v. 22). This isn't about vanity; it's about the trust we've earned through consistent character. Our words, over time, construct either credibility or a wall of doubt around us.

As you reflect on your own speech today, where do you sense the Holy Spirit inviting you to greater wisdom—perhaps in listening more deeply before responding, or in choosing words that heal rather than harm?
com.s:
Proverbs 18 constitutes a collection of discrete wisdom sayings within the second major section of the book (10:1–22:16), traditionally attributed to Solomon. This compilation reflects the educational traditions of ancient Israelite sages who served in royal and scribal contexts, transmitting practical wisdom for navigating social, economic, and spiritual dimensions of life. The chapter exhibits the characteristic parallelism of Hebrew poetry, employing both antithetical and synonymous structures to convey its teachings with memorable force.

The chapter opens with a penetrating observation about the antisocial nature of those who isolate themselves, using the Hebrew term *niphrad* (one who separates himself) to describe someone who pursues selfish desires and quarrels against all sound judgment. This stands in deliberate tension with the book's broader emphasis on community and counsel. Verse 4 employs the evocative metaphor of deep waters (*mayim amuqqim*) to characterize human speech, suggesting both profundity and potential obscurity, while the fountain of wisdom (*meqor ḥokmah*) represents life-giving clarity.

Particularly significant is verse 10, which declares the name of Yahweh a strong tower (*migdal-oz*), into which the righteous run and find safety. This theological affirmation interrupts the predominantly practical orientation of the surrounding verses, grounding wisdom ultimately in covenant relationship with God. The juxtaposition with verse 11, which notes that the wealthy consider their riches a fortified city, creates an implicit critique of misplaced security.

Verse 21 introduces the concept that death and life reside in the power of the tongue (*lashon*), a theme reverberating throughout Proverbs and the broader wisdom tradition. The Hebrew term conveys the instrument of speech as possessing almost autonomous destructive or creative potential. Interpreters debate whether verse 22 concerning finding a wife (*ishah*) refers to marriage generally or to a particular kind of spouse, though the context suggests the former, affirming marriage as divine blessing.

The chapter concludes with observations about friendship and social relationships, notably the famous declaration in verse 24 that a true friend (*ohev*) sticks closer than a brother, though textual difficulties in the first half of this verse have generated considerable scholarly discussion regarding the precise reading and translation.
com.p:
Proverbs 18 emerges from the golden age of Israel's united monarchy, composed under Solomon's reign approximately 950 years before Christ's incarnation. This places the text firmly in the Kingdom era of redemptive history, that brief epoch when God's promises to David were fresh and the temple stood as heaven's dwelling on earth. Yet even in this moment of national glory, wisdom literature was preparing Israel—and through Israel, all nations—for a greater Kingdom and a wiser King who would one day embody every principle here inscribed.

The chapter opens with a sobering portrait of the isolated fool who "separates himself" and "rages against all sound wisdom." Here stands the anti-type of the communal life God has always intended for His image-bearers. From Eden's garden fellowship to the gathered assembly at Sinai to the church as Christ's body, God's redemptive purpose moves toward communion, not isolation. The self-seeking fool prefigures all who reject the wisdom that comes down from above, choosing their own counsel over the divine Word that proceeds from the Father's mouth.

Most striking is the declaration that "the name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run into it and are safe." For Israel under Solomon, the Lord's name was associated with the temple, God's dwelling place on Zion. Yet this proverb whispers of something—Someone—greater. When the eternal Word took flesh, He became the true strong tower, the refuge into which all who call upon His name may flee. What was promised in proverbial form found its fulfillment when Jesus declared Himself the door, the way, the life itself. The tower is no longer a theological abstraction but a Person with nail-scarred hands.

The chapter's teaching on the tongue—"death and life are in the power of the tongue"—carries eschatological weight. James would later call the tongue a fire set ablaze by hell itself. Yet at Pentecost, tongues of fire descended to sanctify human speech for gospel proclamation. The same instrument that brings death became the vehicle of eternal life as apostolic preaching opened the Kingdom to all nations.

For the church awaiting Christ's return, Proverbs 18 calls us to embody wisdom's community, to take refuge in the Name above all names, and to steward our words as bearers of life until He comes whose speech will finally judge the living and the dead.
